clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive axonal (type 2) Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease caused by biallelic mutations in IGHMBP2, encoding immunoglobulin mu-binding protein 2.
Allelic with SMARD1 (spinal muscular atrophy with respiratory distress type 1); IGHMBP2 defines a phenotypic spectrum, with CMT2S at the milder, later-onset end.
Usually presents in infancy or early childhood with distal, predominantly motor weakness that often begins in the legs and later involves the hands.
Unlike classic SMARD1, severe infantile diaphragmatic palsy and early respiratory failure are usually absent, but milder or later respiratory involvement can occur and warrants monitoring.
The amount of residual IGHMBP2 function broadly correlates with severity, with more preserved function favouring the CMT2S phenotype over lethal SMARD1.
Nerve conduction studies show an axonal, motor-predominant pattern.
Distal wasting, foot deformity and areflexia develop as in other axonal CMT subtypes.
Confirming that both alleles carry pathogenic variants is essential given the recessive inheritance.
reference.pathophysiology: IGHMBP2 encodes immunoglobulin mu-binding protein 2, an ATP-dependent superfamily-1 helicase implicated in messenger RNA processing and translation, associating with ribosomes and the translational machinery. Biallelic loss-of-function mutations reduce helicase activity, and the degree of residual function correlates with severity: near-complete loss produces severe infantile SMARD1, with motor neuron loss and diaphragmatic paralysis, whereas hypomorphic variant combinations produce the milder, predominantly axonal neuropathy designated CMT2S. Motor neurons and their long axons appear particularly sensitive to impaired IGHMBP2-dependent translation, giving a length-dependent, motor-predominant axonopathy that sits at the more favourable end of a single gene's clinical continuum.
additionalDifferentials: SMARD1, the severe allelic phenotype of the same gene
Other autosomal recessive axonal CMT subtypes (CMT2B1 LMNA, CMT2B2 MED25)
Autosomal recessive demyelinating CMT4 subtypes when demyelinating features are queried
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies and electromyography demonstrating an axonal, motor-predominant pattern
Gene panel or exome sequencing including IGHMBP2 with confirmation of biallelic variants
Respiratory assessment including diaphragmatic function and evaluation for sleep-related hypoventilation
Parental carrier testing and segregation analysis
SMN1 dosage testing to exclude spinal muscular atrophy
Clinical genetics referral and genetic counselling
redFlags: Any diaphragmatic weakness, nocturnal hypoventilation or respiratory distress, which should be sought actively
Rapidly progressive weakness in infancy suggesting the severe SMARD1 end of the spectrum
Feeding difficulty or failure to thrive in a young child
reference.prognosis: CMT2S generally has a more favourable course than SMARD1, with slowly progressive distal weakness; nonetheless respiratory status should be monitored because the same gene can produce ventilatory compromise, and outcome varies with residual enzyme function.
pitfalls: Assuming every IGHMBP2 phenotype is lethal SMARD1 and not recognising the milder CMT2S end of the spectrum.
Failing to screen respiratory and diaphragmatic function because the presentation looks like uncomplicated CMT.
Missing the recessive inheritance and not confirming that both alleles are affected.
Confusing early distal weakness with spinal muscular atrophy without dedicated SMN1 testing.
management: No disease-specific pharmacotherapy; supportive and rehabilitative care through a paediatric neuromuscular multidisciplinary team
Respiratory monitoring for diaphragmatic weakness and sleep-related hypoventilation, with non-invasive ventilation if ventilatory compromise emerges
Physiotherapy and ankle-foot orthoses for distal, predominantly motor weakness and foot drop
Occupational therapy and developmental support for the child, with adaptive aids as the hands become involved
Neuropathic pain management where sensory symptoms occur
Avoidance of neurotoxic drugs such as vincristine
Autosomal recessive genetic counselling with parental carrier testing and family screening
